content.thinking:
I'm laying out the core facts of the postmortem: all 240 shopper totals fail to reconcile, with the widest discrepancy and oldest affected purchase noted, and the integrity check cadence. I'm also noting that no service errors were observed and no customer loss occurred yet, though shoppers' monthly statements would render the shortfall.

Now I'm tracing the causal chain: the symptom is purchases reconciling short against stored totals (AL1), which traces back to a rollout path leaving total_this_month_cents unmoved while in-month purchases accumulated (F1, U4, U5), and further back to a feature flag enabling the derive-the-month path at a specific point, with deploys ruled out as a cause.

I'm confirming the flag change at T13 is the only earlier change in the window, with no deploys recorded (T8, T9). The replica restart at T7 happened after onset (AL1 dates first harm earlier), so it can't be a prior cause—it's a later event, not something that could trigger what already started.

Now I'm structuring the explanation: the symptom from AL1, then the stored month totals falling short because purchases weren't adding to total_this_month_cents (per F1, U4, U5), then tracing that those purchases ran through record_purchase_deriving_the_month, which gets called by record_a_purchase when derive_the_month is true.

This function updated history and total_cents but omitted the total_this_month_cents update that the default path performs for in_current_month purchases (F1) — that's the root mechanism. I'm deciding on ordering: symptom first, then the omission in the rollout path, then why that path was active (the flag switched on at P1, per P1 and T13).

Now I can state the root cause clearly: on the path the monthly-spend feature selects, record_a_purchase calls the version that derives the month, and that function appends the purchase and updates total_cents but never adds it to total_this_month_cents like the default path does — so switching on the feature silently made stored monthly totals come out lower than what was actually purchased. In plain terms, the new flag broke the running monthly total, and that damage persists since statements and averages still read from the stale stored value while the flag remains on.

I also note a contributing factor: the spend-integrity check only runs every several days, so the fault could run unseen for a while before detection — I should flag this as something to address with more frequent monitoring.

Another gap is the missing test coverage: no test exercised record_a_purchase with the derive-month flag against reconciliation before the fault surfaced, though the eventual fix patch does add such tests, so that's covered by the review/merge fix.

Then there's the rollout issue — the flag was switched on in production without any check comparing month totals beforehand, and no reconciliation run is visible immediately after the flip; this overlaps with the monitoring-frequency factor, so I might combine them into one broader recommendation about tying integrity checks to flag changes.

Lastly, nobody was paged — an alert fired but no on-call incident was linked, and even though Argus itself resolved things quickly, the human escalation path was effectively unused, which could be worth flagging as a process gap: pages should go to on-call when stored-value systems like this one misbehave.

For action items, I'm thinking the repair step should run the monthly totals repair script in dry-run first, review the negative-gap accounts it surfaces, then apply it for real with --apply once the fix is deployed or the flag is disabled, writing the corrections back to the account store.

On detection, I want to increase the spend-integrity check frequency to answer CF-1, and trigger a reconciliation run whenever the monthly-spend feature or related flags change, which covers CF-3. For process, paging on-call on the SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile alert addresses CF-4. I'm also wondering whether shoppers may have already seen monthly statements rendered from the short totals.

For what went well, Argus read the flag history and correctly tied the onset to the flag change, and Code-Fix drafted PR #346 shortly after the alert, though the investigator placed onset earlier. Argus declined to act without verification and instead recommended reverting the flag. For what went wrong, the lack of paging is already a contributing factor, so I shouldn't duplicate it, and I'm weighing whether not reading the logs counts as a response gap rather than a limitation of the record.

For what got lucky, I'm noting customer takings weren't affected despite the short totals, and that the fault stayed isolated to stored totals without cascading into other failures like division errors.

Noting my assumptions: onset dated to the oldest affected purchase per AL1, duration as a lower bound, mechanism inferred from code review, and flag state after T13 unverified. On the "240 of 240" figure, I should flag that it may represent only checked totals rather than a full sample. For ruling out causes, deploys in the window weren't logged, and the pod restart came after onset per AL1's dating, so it's correctly excluded as a later rather than earlier change.

I also need to pin down the symptom description precisely — something like "no failures were seen; stored shopper monthly spend totals came out short of purchases" — while being careful not to overstate that failure rates were actually measured.

For the cause chain, step 1 should point to AL1, and step 2 should bring in F1, U4, and U5, with the framing being that reconciliation never happened and the widest shortfall traces back to a specific figure. I'll also note the PR reference and its timing relative to the alert for the "went well" section.

action_items.item: Once the fix is deployed or monthly-spend-feature is off, run scripts/repair_monthly_totals.py without --apply and review the corrections it prints.
Run scripts/repair_monthly_totals.py with --apply and apply the corrections file it writes to the account store.
Look into the accounts the repair script lists with a negative gap, which it leaves unchanged.
Run the spend-integrity check more often than every {A5} days.
Run the spend-totals reconciliation automatically after any change to monthly-spend-feature or any other flag that changes how purchases are recorded.
Route SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile to the on-call rotation so it pages a person.

causal_chain.step: No failures were seen. Instead, the spend-integrity check found that {A1} of {A2} checked shopper totals did not match the purchases behind them. The widest was short by {A3}, and the oldest affected purchase was recorded at {A4}.

The stored month total, `total_this_month_cents`, fell below the sum of the account's current-month purchases, which is what the reconciliation compares it with. According to Code-Fix's reading, each current-month purchase recorded through `record_purchase_deriving_the_month` was added to the history and to `total_cents` but not to `total_this_month_cents`. The default `record_purchase` adds it when `purchase.in_current_month` is true.

ruled_out.what: A deploy: no deploy came back from the production change events read for the window before the alert. The only change read was the flag change.
The replica restarts at {T7.2}: they came after the first harm, which the alert dates at {A4}.

causal_chain.step: Purchases took that path because the feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on at {P1.1}. That flag makes `record_a_purchase` run with `derive_the_month=True`, which calls `record_purchase_deriving_the_month`. The first mis-totalled purchase came {began - P1.1} later. The flag provider's history shows this as the only flag change by anyone but Argus in the hour before the onset.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Turning on a new feature likely made the shop stop adding each new purchase to the shopper's running total for the month, so stored monthly totals came out lower than what shoppers had actually bought.

contributing_factors.factor: The spend-integrity check, the only thing in the record that found the fault, runs only every {A5} days. Wrong totals could build up unseen for up to that long.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A check that ran more often would have found the short totals soon after the flag went on, so fewer would have been written.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No test was seen that ran `record_a_purchase` with `derive_the_month=True` and checked the month total against the purchases. Code-Fix's patch adds such cases.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A test like that would likely have failed on the old `record_purchase_deriving_the_month` before the flag went on in production.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: No reconciliation of stored spend totals was seen running after monthly-spend-feature was switched on.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Checking totals right after the flag change would have shown short totals within the first purchases, not days later.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

contributing_factors.factor: The SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile alert pages nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A paged person could have put the flag back as soon as Argus recommended it, which would have stopped new short totals sooner.
contributing_factors.label: CF-4

went_well: Argus tied the onset to the only flag change in the hour before it by reading the flag provider's history.
Argus did not take an action it had no way to check in time. It recommended putting monthly-spend-feature back and left that to a person.
Code-Fix opened a draft fix as PR #346 {T18.1 - alert_raised} after the alert. It comes with tests and a separate repair script for the totals already written.

input.root_cause: When monthly-spend-feature is on, `record_a_purchase` takes the `derive_the_month=True` path and calls `record_purchase_deriving_the_month`. That function added the purchase to the history and to `total_cents` but never added a current-month purchase to `total_this_month_cents`, which the default `record_purchase` does. So each current-month purchase recorded on that path left the stored month total short by that purchase's price.
input.still_at_risk: The short monthly totals already written are still wrong in storage, where monthly statements and per-purchase averages read them, and any current-month purchase recorded while the flag is on can write another short total.
input.symptom: No failures were seen, but stored shopper monthly spend totals came out short of their purchases.
